questions.question: What is CSRF and how does Spring Security protect against it?
questions.title: CSRF — What It Is and Spring Security CSRF Protection
questions.direct_answer: **Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** tricks an authenticated user's browser into making an unintended state-changing request, exploiting the fact that **browsers automatically attach cookies**. Spring Security defaults to the **Synchronizer Token Pattern**: a per-session token that must accompany every state-changing request as a hidden form field or `X-CSRF-TOKEN` header. **CSRF only matters when authentication uses cookies** — for stateless JWT APIs (token in `Authorization` header), `csrf().disable()` is correct because cross-origin JS cannot set arbitrary headers. Modern browsers add `SameSite=Lax|Strict` cookies as a layered defense.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the session-cookie dependency of CSRF and the correct trade-offs between enabling/disabling CSRF protection.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Disabling CSRF in Spring Security for all applications without understanding that it's only safe to disable for truly stateless APIs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Synchronizer Token Pattern vs Double Submit Cookie pattern, and why SameSite=Strict cookie attribute is a modern mitigation.

sections.title: CSRF Only Matters With Cookie Auth
sections.content:
**CSRF exploits one specific browser behavior**: cookies attach to requests automatically, no JavaScript needed.
- When a user is logged into `bank.com`, a malicious page at `evil.com` can submit `<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">`.
- The browser attaches the bank's session cookie automatically — `bank.com` receives an authenticated request the user never intended.

**CSRF is only relevant with cookie-based authentication.** If your API uses JWT in the `Authorization` header, CSRF is not a threat — headers require explicit JS, and cross-origin JS is blocked by same-origin policy. **`csrf.disable()` is correct for stateless JWT APIs and incorrect for session-based apps.** Tutorials saying "disable CSRF for REST" are right *for stateless APIs*; copying that into a session-based app creates a real vulnerability.

Spring Security uses the **Synchronizer Token Pattern** by default. It generates a random token, stores it server-side, and requires it in every state-changing request (POST/PUT/DELETE) as a form field or custom header. Cross-origin attackers can't forge it — they can't read the session or first-party cookie containing it.

The **Double Submit Cookie** pattern (`CookieCsrfTokenRepository`) is the SPA-friendly alternative — token in a JS-readable cookie + same value in `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header.

sections.title: Three Patterns: Synchronizer, Double Submit, SameSite
sections.content:
**Synchronizer Token (server-side storage):**
- Spring generates a per-session token
- Thymeleaf injects automatically: `<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="...">`
- For SPAs: token via `/api/csrf` or meta tag, sent as `X-CSRF-TOKEN` header
- Default for session-based Spring Security apps

**Double Submit Cookie (`CookieCsrfTokenRepository`):**
- Spring sets token in a cookie that JS can read (not `HttpOnly`)
- SPA reads cookie, sends value as `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header
- Angular `HttpClientXsrfModule` and Axios support this automatically
- Standard choice for SPAs — no extra API call, cookie always available

```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf
            .csrfTokenRepository(CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()))
        .build();
}
```

**`SameSite` cookie attribute (browser-level CSRF defense):**
- `SameSite=Lax` (Chrome 80+ default) — blocks cookies on cross-site POST and AJAX
- `SameSite=Strict` — blocks on all cross-site requests, even link navigation
- Configure: `server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=lax`
- With `Lax`/`Strict`, CSRF token becomes redundant for modern browsers — keep tokens for IE compatibility or defense in depth

sections.title: When to Disable CSRF (and When Not To)
sections.content:
**Rule:** CSRF protection is required when authentication uses cookies. Otherwise it adds overhead with no benefit.

**Safe to disable CSRF:**
- Purely stateless APIs with JWT in `Authorization` header
- APIs consumed only by server-to-server clients (no browser)
- Internal microservices behind an API gateway with OAuth2 client credentials
- Mobile backends where the client explicitly sets `Authorization`

**CSRF must remain enabled:**
- Session-based web apps (browsers send cookies automatically)
- APIs where JWT is stored in cookies (even `HttpOnly`)
- Apps serving authenticated web pages and API endpoints from the same origin
- Any endpoint browsers might call with cookies attached

**The hybrid trap:**
- App uses session for web UI and JWT for API, sharing one `SecurityFilterChain`
- Disabling CSRF globally (for the JWT API) leaves the web UI exposed
- **Correct approach**: two `SecurityFilterChain` beans — one for `/api/**` (stateless, CSRF off), one for the UI (sessions, CSRF on)

**Cookie-stored JWT:**
- Choosing `HttpOnly` cookie over `localStorage` blocks XSS theft
- Inherits CSRF risk — keep CSRF enabled with `SameSite=Lax` + token combo

**SameSite simplifies the decision:**
- `SameSite=Strict` -> CSRF impossible without tokens (modern browsers)
- `SameSite=Lax` -> blocks cross-site state-changing methods
- `server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=strict` in Spring Boot

sections.title: Selective CSRF and Common Disable Mistakes
sections.content:
**The common mistake target:**
- Devs disable CSRF globally with `http.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)` for all Spring Boot apps
- Without understanding when it's appropriate
- Result: session-based UI now CSRF-vulnerable

**When CSRF is necessary:**
- App uses session cookies and is accessed by browsers
- Server-rendered HTML apps
- Any app where browsers send credentials on cross-origin requests

**When CSRF can be disabled:**
- Stateless API with JWT in `Authorization` header
- Browsers don't auto-send `Authorization` headers cross-origin
- Attacker's page can't include a JWT it doesn't have
- Caveat: switch to cookie-based JWT later -> re-enable CSRF

**Selective CSRF for hybrid apps (Spring Security 6+):**
- Two `SecurityFilterChain` beans matched by URL pattern
- `/api/**` chain: CSRF disabled, stateless
- `/web/**` chain: CSRF enabled, session-based
- Or use `csrf.requireCsrfProtectionMatcher(...)` to limit which paths require token

**Configuration sketch:**

```java
@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .csrf(c -> c.disable())
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .build();
}

@Bean
@Order(2)
SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .build();
}
```

sections.title: CSRF Defenses: When and What to Watch
sections.content:
**When Synchronizer Token helps:**
- Server-rendered Spring MVC/Thymeleaf apps
- Maximum browser compatibility (works in legacy)
- Defense in depth even with `SameSite`

**When Double Submit Cookie helps:**
- SPAs (React/Angular/Vue) with cookie-based session
- No need for explicit token-fetch endpoint
- Frameworks like Angular auto-handle

**When SameSite alone helps:**
- Modern browser audience (no IE)
- Simplifies architecture
- Catches CSRF before it reaches the app

**When it hurts:**
- Disabling CSRF on session-based UI -> direct vulnerability
- `SameSite=Strict` breaks legitimate cross-site flows (OAuth callbacks, payment redirects)
- CSRF token endpoints leak via timing if not protected
- Mixing token + cookie patterns inconsistently

**Watch for:**
- **Login CSRF** — pre-auth CSRF tokens are still needed for the login form
- **Logout CSRF** — attackers logging users out is annoying; protect logout too
- **Multipart/file uploads** — token must be in form field, not header
- **WebSocket upgrades** — `Origin` check, not CSRF token
- **OAuth2 redirect callbacks** — `state` parameter is the equivalent CSRF defense
- **`SameSite=Strict` and SSO** — IdP redirects may break; use `Lax` for SSO flows

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CSRF exploits browser automatic cookie sending** — JWTs in `Authorization` headers are immune.
- **Spring Security enables CSRF by default** for session-based apps via Synchronizer Token Pattern.
- **SPAs use `CookieCsrfTokenRepository`** — token in JS-readable cookie + `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header.
- **`SameSite=Strict|Lax` is a modern alternative** — browser blocks cross-site cookie attachment, eliminating the attack vector.
- **`http.csrf().disable()` is correct only for stateless JWT APIs** — never for session-cookie apps.
- **Hybrid apps** — use two `SecurityFilterChain` beans, one per auth model.
- **Login and logout endpoints** still need CSRF protection even before/after the main session.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**How the attack works**
- User logged into `bank.com` with session cookie
- Attacker page `evil.com` contains `<form action='https://bank.com/transfer' method='POST'>`
- User visits `evil.com`; browser submits form including the bank cookie
- Bank sees a valid session cookie and processes the transfer

**Spring Security's defense — Synchronizer Token Pattern**
- Server generates a CSRF token per session, embeds in forms as hidden field
- POST/PUT/DELETE — Spring validates submitted token matches session token
- `evil.com` can't read the bank's CSRF token (same-origin policy) — forged form lacks it

**For SPAs**
- `CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()`
- Token written to cookie that SPA JS can read
- SPA sends `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header on every mutating request

**When to disable**
- Stateless JWT API: no session cookie -> no CSRF vector
- `http.csrf().disable()` is safe and correct
- Don't blindly copy this into session-based apps

**Modern simplification**
- `SameSite=Lax` (browser default) blocks cross-site POST cookies
- `SameSite=Strict` blocks all cross-site cookie attachment
- `server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=lax`
- Combine with token for defense in depth

**Hybrid apps**
- Two `SecurityFilterChain` beans
- `/api/**` stateless + CSRF disabled
- Web UI session + CSRF enabled

**Don't forget**
- Login CSRF — pre-auth token still needed for login form
- OAuth2 redirect callback uses `state` parameter, not CSRF token
- Multipart uploads — token in form field, not header

questions.question: How do you correctly configure CORS in a Spring Security application?
questions.title: CORS Configuration with Spring Security
questions.direct_answer: CORS must be configured **in Spring Security**, not just in Spring MVC, because the security filter chain intercepts requests before they reach `DispatcherServlet`. **Enable CORS in `SecurityFilterChain` with `.cors(...)`**, then define allowed origins, methods, and headers in a **`CorsConfigurationSource`** bean. Without this, **preflight `OPTIONS` requests are rejected with 401/403** before reaching MVC config — the most common CORS bug. **`allowCredentials(true)` is incompatible with wildcard origins** — enumerate exact origins or use `allowedOriginPatterns`. **CORS is browser-only**; backend-to-backend calls ignore it entirely.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the interaction between the security filter chain and CORS — a common source of production bugs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only adding @CrossOrigin on controllers or configuring WebMvcConfigurer and wondering why the API still returns CORS errors in production.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why preflight OPTIONS requests carry no credentials and must be permitted, and discuss environment-specific CORS policies.

sections.title: Why @CrossOrigin Alone Doesn't Work
sections.content:
The most common CORS bug in Spring Security apps: developers add `@CrossOrigin` to controllers, errors persist, hours wasted before realizing **Spring Security's filter chain rejected the request before it ever reached MVC**.

The sequence: HTTP request -> Servlet container -> `DelegatingFilterProxy` -> **Spring Security filter chain** -> `DispatcherServlet` -> Controller. Spring Security runs **before** MVC. If the security chain rejects (which it does for unauthenticated `OPTIONS` preflights), the request never reaches `@CrossOrigin`.

**Preflight OPTIONS** is how browsers check CORS permissions before non-simple requests (PUT, DELETE, JSON content-type, custom headers).
- The OPTIONS asks: "does this server allow cross-origin requests from my origin with these methods/headers?" **OPTIONS carries no credentials** — no cookies, no `Authorization` — because the browser is just asking permission.
- Spring Security sees an unauthenticated OPTIONS, returns **401**, and the browser interprets that as "CORS denied" and blocks the actual request.

**Fix:** configure CORS in the security chain with `http.cors(...)` so Spring Security runs the CORS filter **before** authentication filters, allowing valid preflights through without auth. The `CorsConfigurationSource` bean defines what's actually permitted.

sections.title: CORS Preflight OPTIONS Check
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    browser["Browser at app.example.com"] --> request["fetch PUT api.example.com/orders/42 with JSON body and Authorization header"]
    request --> nonSimple{"Non-simple? Method not GET/POST/HEAD or content-type not form-encoded or has custom headers"}
    nonSimple -->|simple| direct["Skip preflight, send directly"]
    nonSimple -->|non-simple| pre["Send OPTIONS preflight: Origin app.example.com Access-Control-Request-Method PUT Access-Control-Request-Headers Authorization Content-Type"]
    pre --> spring["Spring Security CorsFilter (must be in chain via http.cors)"]
    spring --> check{"Origin allowed? Method allowed? Headers allowed?"}
    check -->|No| reject["403 / missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin -> browser blocks actual request"]
    check -->|Yes| ok["200 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin app.example.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods PUT Access-Control-Allow-Headers Authorization Content-Type Access-Control-Max-Age 3600"]
    ok --> cache["Browser caches preflight up to max-age"]
    cache --> direct
    direct --> auth["Spring Security auth filters -> controller"]
```

sections.title: Wire CORS Into the Security Filter Chain
sections.content:
**Spring Security's CORS integration:**
- Registers a `CorsFilter` before authentication filters
- Preflight `OPTIONS` is handled by `CorsFilter`, returns 200 with CORS headers — no auth check

**Minimal config:**

```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .cors(cors -> cors.configurationSource(corsConfigurationSource()))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.OPTIONS, "/**").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .build();
}
```

**Two ways to point at the source:**
- `Customizer.withDefaults()` — Spring auto-wires a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean
- `.configurationSource(corsConfigurationSource())` — explicit, clearer with multiple chains

**The `permitAll()` for OPTIONS is belt-and-suspenders:**
- Explicitly allows all OPTIONS without auth
- Some configurations need this even with `http.cors()`
- Costs nothing; prevents subtle misconfig fallback to requiring auth on OPTIONS

**Where things go wrong without `http.cors()`:**
- `@CrossOrigin` on controllers — ignored by Spring Security filter chain
- `WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings()` alone — runs after security, OPTIONS already rejected

sections.title: CorsConfigurationSource Bean — The Real Configuration
Environment-Specific Policies and Debugging
sections.content:
**Inject origins from configuration per environment:**

```java
@Value("${cors.allowed-origins}")
private List<String> allowedOrigins;

@Bean
public CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
    CorsConfiguration config = new CorsConfiguration();
    config.setAllowedOrigins(allowedOrigins);
    return source;
}
```

```yaml
# application.yml (dev)
cors.allowed-origins: http://localhost:3000

# application-prod.yml
cors.allowed-origins: https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com
```

**Production rules:**
- Never use wildcard `*` with credentials in production
- Wildcard signals the policy wasn't designed carefully
- Enumerate specific origins per environment

**Debugging CORS errors:**

```bash
curl -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/endpoint \
  -H "Origin: https://app.example.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization,Content-Type" \
  -v
```

- Response should include `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Allow-Methods`, `Allow-Headers`
- If any are missing or wrong, the browser blocks the actual request
- Check exact case-sensitive match of `Origin` header value

**For microservices:**
- Configure CORS at the API gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, AWS API Gateway)
- Disable or relax in individual services
- Services receive requests only from gateway -> same-domain -> CORS not needed per-service

sections.title: CORS Strategy: Helps, Hurts, Watch For
sections.content:
**When CORS helps:**
- SPAs hosted on a separate domain from the API
- Multi-tenant apps with subdomains needing API access
- Public APIs intended for browser consumption

**When it hurts:**
- Same-origin app where API and UI share host -> no CORS needed
- Mobile apps (no browser, no CORS) -> often misconfigured for nothing
- Backend-to-backend services (CORS doesn't apply)

**Watch for:**
- **Don't ship `allowedOrigins("*")` in production** with credentials
- **`allowedOriginPatterns` for subdomain wildcards** — `https://*.example.com`
- **`maxAge(3600)`** to cache preflights and reduce traffic
- **`exposedHeaders`** for any custom response headers the SPA needs to read (e.g., `X-Total-Count`, `Location`)
- **CORS at the gateway, not per-service** for microservices
- **`OPTIONS` must `permitAll`** — otherwise auth filter blocks before CORS filter
- **CSRF + CORS interaction** — CSRF tokens still needed for cookie-based auth even with CORS
- **WebSocket** — uses `Origin` header check, not CORS
- **Browser dev tools** — Network tab + Console show exact failure reason; rely on those, not blind config changes

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Security runs before `DispatcherServlet`** — preflight OPTIONS rejected at security chain never reaches MVC's CORS config.
- **Configure CORS in `SecurityFilterChain` via `http.cors()`** — points to a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean.
- **Preflight OPTIONS carries no credentials** — must be permitted; `permitAll()` for OPTIONS as belt-and-suspenders.
- **`allowCredentials(true)` conflicts with `allowedOrigins("*")`** — use `allowedOriginPatterns("https://*.example.com")`.
- **CORS is browser-only** — `curl` and microservice-to-microservice ignore it; CORS protects only browser JS.
- **`maxAge(3600)`** caches preflight, reduces traffic.
- **For microservices**, configure CORS at the API gateway, not per-service.
